d.title: Three descriptions of the same tool, and what the model can tell from each
d.caption: The description is the only part of a tool definition that answers **when to use this**, and the third row is the only one that does. An empty description leaves the model guessing from the function name; an accurate one-liner says what the tool *is* and nothing about *when*. The other half of the same problem is overlap: **if `search_docs` and `search_tickets` both say "search for information", the model is choosing at random**, and no amount of instruction in the system prompt fixes a specification problem.

d.title: A constraint in the schema is a request and a guarantee
d.caption: Exactly 1.5's argument in a different place. `top_k` declared with `ge=1, le=20` appears **in the schema the model sees**, so it is told the range — and is **validated on the way back**, so a model asking for 500 results gets a `ValidationError` rather than an expensive query. The prompt-text version of the same constraint does only the first half and gives you no signal when it was ignored.

d.title: A tool's error message is prompt, because the model reads it
d.caption: `ToolException: user_id must be numeric, got 'alice'` goes back into the transcript, **so the model reads it** — and either fixes its argument or explains the problem to the user. Which makes the wording of a tool's failure a prompt-engineering decision rather than a logging one: **"invalid input" tells the model nothing it can act on, and naming the constraint and the offending value tells it exactly what to change.**

d.title: The transcript shape a tool call produces
d.caption: Three messages for one tool round, and the middle one is the shape worth memorising: **an `AIMessage` whose content is empty and whose `tool_calls` carries the request.** The `ToolMessage` answering it is tied back by `tool_call_id`, not by position — which is what §03 is about, because the ids are the only thing connecting a request to its answer when there are several.

d.title: The error arrives one step after the mistake
d.caption: If an `AIMessage` contains two tool calls and you append only one `ToolMessage`, the conversation is malformed — and **the failure does not happen when you build the list.** It happens on the **next** model call, when the provider rejects a transcript containing an unanswered call id. That displacement is what makes it hard to debug: **the error names the unanswered id rather than the code path that skipped it**, and the usual cause is a loop that `break`s or `continue`s on the first failure. The rule is mechanical: **one ToolMessage per call, including the ones that failed.**

d.title: Four settings, and the one that is about side effects rather than choice
d.caption: The first three constrain **which** tool; the fourth constrains **how many at once**. `parallel_tool_calls=False` is the one to reach for when calls have side effects or order matters — two concurrent writes to the same record is a correctness problem that no amount of tool-choice tuning addresses. And `"any"` is the setting for when **answering from memory is never acceptable**, which is 3.7's failure 4 made impossible by construction.

d.title: 2n + 2 messages, n + 1 model calls
d.caption: Each tool round adds **exactly two** messages — the model's request and the tool's answer — and the final answer adds one more. So the arithmetic is fixed: **a run with n tool rounds produces 2n + 2 messages and invokes the model n + 1 times.** Which is the formula to have when reading a bill or a trace, because it turns "the agent took a while" into a number of model calls you can check against the transcript length.

d.title: Every model call re-sends the whole transcript
d.caption: Call 1 sends 1 message, call 2 sends 3, call 3 sends 5 — **the accumulated list, every time.** Which has a consequence worth stating plainly: **a tool returning a lot of text is expensive out of proportion to its usefulness**, because the result rides in every subsequent call. A tool that returns a 40 KB document and is used on step one is paid for again on steps two, three and four. 3.5 shows the same shape for conversation history and 13.1 prices it properly.

steps.note: a big tool result is paid for n times

d.title: Three things missing, and all three are in 3.7
d.caption: The hand-written loop is worth writing **once**, so that every prebuilt agent afterwards is recognisable and so that when one misbehaves you know what it is doing. These three gaps are why you should not ship it. The first is the one with the misleading symptom: **a model that always asks for a tool never terminates**, and 3.7 shows that it fails with an error about *length* rather than about looping.

d.title: Two names, and the overwhelming majority of material online uses the deprecated one
d.caption: `create_react_agent` from `langgraph.prebuilt` emits a deprecation notice pointing at `from langchain.agents import create_agent`, **deprecated in LangGraph V1.0 and due for removal in V2.0.** So you will encounter both names — and the thing worth knowing is the proportion: **almost everything you find online uses the deprecated one**, which is why a tutorial often will not match your imports, and why new code should use the new name even though search results argue otherwise.

d.title: Five middleware, all of them cross-cutting concerns the loop body would otherwise carry
d.caption: Middleware runs **around each model call and each tool call inside the loop**, which is the only place several of these can work at all. Summarisation has to happen *before* each model call, not once at the start. Human-in-the-loop has to interrupt *between* a decision and its execution. And tool gating has to filter the tool list *per user* at the moment the model is asked, which no static construction can do.

d.title: Cost is quadratic in turns, because each turn re-sends everything before it
d.caption: The last prompt grows linearly — 300 characters a turn — and **the cumulative total grows quadratically**, because every turn re-sends the whole history. Twenty turns is 12,760 characters of input; a hundred turns is **303,800, which is 24× the twenty-turn figure for 5× the conversation.** That is the shape to recognise, because it means a conversation-length problem looks mild in testing and severe in production, where the long conversations live.

d.title: Cost degrades gracefully; the context window does not
d.caption: **Cost gets expensive, someone notices, you fix it.** The context window does not work that way: once the buffer exceeds it the request **fails outright** — and it fails **on the longest conversations first**, which are by definition the ones belonging to users getting the most value from the product. So the failure is both sudden and adversely selected, which is a worse combination than either property alone.

d.title: Three strategies, and none of them loses nothing
d.caption: **There is no strategy that loses nothing**, which makes this a product decision rather than a technical one — you are choosing which kind of forgetting your users will meet. Trimming loses **early facts**: a name, an id, a constraint stated once. Summarising loses **specifics**: numbers, names and exact wording become a paraphrase. Retrieval loses nothing in principle and adds a lookup that can surface the wrong turn. 3.6 implements the first, 13.3 the second and 13.4 the third.

d.title: Two messages per turn, stored
d.caption: Three turns in, six messages out — the history store holds the human and AI message from each turn, in order, and nothing else. Which is the baseline that makes 3.5's arithmetic concrete: **the store is append-only and nothing in it is ever smaller than it was**, so every trimming or summarisation strategy is a thing you do to this list on the way to the model rather than a thing the store does for you.

d.title: Worth understanding anyway, for the same reason as the hand-written loop
d.caption: `RunnableWithMessageHistory` is deprecated in favour of a LangGraph checkpointer, and it is worth understanding **for the same reason 3.3 writes the agent loop by hand**: the graph version does the same job with more machinery, and **knowing what the simple version does makes the richer one legible rather than magical.** Read it once as the definition of what a checkpointer has to provide, then use the checkpointer.

d.title: The system message is the oldest message, so keep-the-last-N drops it first
d.caption: **`include_system=True` pins it, which is almost always what you want** — dropping the instructions to save a few tokens silently changes the behaviour. And the failure is particularly nasty because it is **gradual and correlated with conversation length**: short conversations keep their instructions and behave correctly, long ones lose them and start drifting, so the symptom reads as *"the model gets worse the longer you talk to it"* rather than as a trimming bug. Note the last row: `end_on="human"` kept **four** of the five it was allowed, because trimming to a clean boundary beats trimming to an exact count.

d.title: A runaway loop is a quadratic bill terminating in a misleading error
d.caption: An uncapped loop **does not hang forever in a recognisable way.** It runs until the transcript exceeds the context window and then fails with an error about **length** — so the symptom points at token limits rather than at looping, and the obvious response is to raise a limit that was never the problem. It is expensive on the way there too, because each iteration re-sends a transcript that grew by two messages: **a quadratic bill, ending in a misleading error.** The cap stopped it at 6 calls and 14 messages.

d.title: The guard's message matters as much as its existence
d.caption: A hallucinated tool name needs a guard, and **what the guard says decides whether the run recovers.** Returning `"error: no tool named 'check_inventory'. available: ['calculate', 'lookup_order']"` **gives the model the list**, so it can pick a real one and continue. Returning `"unknown tool"` tells it only that something failed, so its best move is to guess again. Same guard, same cost, and one of them turns a failed run into a completed one.

d.title: One try block, and a far better outcome than a 500
d.caption: This is why 3.1 argued that a tool's error message is prompt. Catch the exception, return its message as the `ToolMessage` content, and **the model reads it, understands what went wrong, and either fixes its argument or explains the problem to the user.** Both of those beat a 500, and the whole mechanism is **one `try` block** — which is the cheapest robustness in this module by a wide margin.

d.title: Every guard in this lesson passes
d.caption: **No exception, no unknown tool, no loop, no malformed transcript.** The model simply answered rather than acting, and the loop did exactly what it was told — a reply with no tool calls means done. It is also **the hardest failure to notice, because the answer claims the tool was used**: *"I looked up order A-1"* reads as evidence of a lookup, so a human reviewing the transcript sees a successful tool-using run unless they check the message list. Two defences apply and neither is a guard: **evaluate the trajectory rather than the answer** (14.7), and **design tools whose output the model cannot plausibly guess.**

d.title: The p50 is not the problem; the gap between p50 and p95 is
d.caption: A single call and a fixed chain have **identical p50 and p95** — they do the same work every time, so there is no tail. A router adds one decision and a small spread. **An agent's p95 is more than twice its p50**, which is the property that matters operationally: you provision for the tail, you are billed for the tail on the requests that hit it, and the tail is where the timeout policy has to be set.

d.title: Five properties given up, and the one that compounds
d.caption: **Testability deserves the emphasis because it compounds.** With a fixed chain you can assert that step two ran with a particular input; with an agent you can only assert on the final answer — which means **every test is an end-to-end test, and a change anywhere can break any of them** for reasons that take a while to locate. The others are costs you can budget for; this one changes how the whole test suite behaves.

d.title: One question, three answers, and the first one is a reminder
d.caption: **If the steps are known in advance, you do not need a model to choose what you already know** — which is the sentence worth carrying out of this module, because the agent is the default people reach for and it is the right answer to only the third row. One decision then a fixed path is a router: cheaper, testable, and with the p50/p95 spread of §01's third row rather than its fourth.
